correct_answer: Require an assignment and assumption agreement (with owner consent per Section 12.1) formally transferring the subcontract from Advanced Mechanical Systems Inc. to AMS Holdings LLC, then accept a waiver from AMS Holdings — and simultaneously obtain the articles of dissolution to confirm Advanced Mechanical no longer exists as a viable entity to sign.
rationale: This is an entity resolution problem with real legal exposure. A lien waiver from an entity that is not party to the subcontract provides no lien protection — if AMS Holdings LLC never formally assumed the contract, their waiver may not extinguish Advanced Mechanical Systems Inc.'s potential lien rights (even if dissolved, a dissolved entity can still have residual claims during wind-down). The correct path is to formalize the assignment: obtain the articles of dissolution proving Advanced Mechanical no longer exists, execute a formal assignment and assumption agreement (requiring owner consent per Section 12.1 of the subcontract), and then accept the waiver from the entity that actually holds the contract obligations. Answer A is wrong because same-principal does not equal same-entity in lien law — courts have consistently held that corporate formalities matter for lien validity. Answer B is impractical and potentially impossible: if Advanced Mechanical was dissolved January 1, it cannot execute new documents (Tony confirmed dissolution in the Teams message, which is the critical hidden signal that makes option B unworkable). Answer D shifts risk but does not eliminate the lien exposure — a GC indemnity does not prevent a lien from being filed, only provides a claim for damages after the fact, and the lender will not accept this for draw purposes.
